Sample text:
---
Mara found the map on the morning the river changed its mind. For thirty years it had run obligingly past the bottom of her garden, silver in winter, brown after rain, always south toward the mills and the sea. That Tuesday she woke to silence, looked out, and saw it flowing north instead, unhurried and certain, as if it had remembered an appointment it had forgotten long ago. Herons stood puzzled on the bank. The moored boats strained gently against ropes pointing the wrong way. And on her kitchen table, where no one could have left it, lay a map of her own town that was almost, but not quite, correct.

The streets were where she expected them to be: Mill Lane, Cinder Row, the crooked alley behind the bakery where cats conducted their parliament at dusk. But there were extras. A narrow bridge crossed the river where no bridge had ever stood, drawn in blue ink still wet to the touch. A library occupied the vacant lot beside the post office. Halfway up Bishop Hill, in careful capital letters, someone had written: HERE THE WIND REMEMBERS YOUR NAME. Beneath that, smaller: Do not fold. Maps remember being folded, and hold grudges about the creases.

Mara was sixty one, retired from the county survey office, and not given to miracles before breakfast. She made tea, because tea was a sensible response to geography misbehaving, and inspected the map through her magnifying glass. The paper smelled of rain and old classrooms. Every time she blinked, a detail altered. A park bench migrated across Green Square. The war memorial turned, very slowly, to face a different direction. The river on the map, unlike the river outside, flowed both ways at once, meeting itself in the middle with a small, polite splash inked in silver.

She should have called someone. The council, perhaps, or her brother in Leeds who collected impossible objects and bad marriages with equal enthusiasm. Instead she put on her coat, tucked the map carefully into a biscuit tin to keep it unfolded, and went out to find the bridge. The town felt ordinary in the way dreams feel ordinary while you are inside them. Mr. Patel raised a hand from his shop doorway. The bakery queue discussed football. No one else seemed to notice that the river had reversed, or that all the clocks on High Street showed different hours, each one confidently wrong.

The bridge was there. That was the first true shock. Stone, moss, a brass rail warm from sun that had not yet risen properly. It arched over the north flowing water to a bank Mara had walked a hundred times, except now a path continued where brambles should have been, winding between trees she did not recognize. Their leaves were pale underneath, like pages. When the breeze moved them they made not a rustle but a murmur, as if many people were reading quietly just out of sight. Halfway across, she stopped. Her name was being said by the wind, exactly as promised, in her mother's voice.

Her mother had been dead eleven years, long enough for grief to become furniture: present in every room, mostly unremarked, occasionally bruising a shin in the dark. She had forgotten, or believed she had forgotten, the precise way her mother said Mara, stretching the first syllable when amused, clipping it when worried. The wind knew both versions. It repeated them among the pale leaves until Mara had to sit down on the bridge, biscuit tin clutched to her chest, laughing and furious. 'You might have called sooner,' she told the water. The water, busy going the wrong way, declined to apologize.

Beyond the trees stood the library from the map, though library is too small a word. It was built from doors. Hundreds of them, thousands perhaps, fitted together into walls and towers: cottage doors with iron latches, grand doors painted green, a submarine hatch, a wardrobe door still smelling faintly of mothballs and winter coats. Each had a brass plate. Mara read the nearest: THE AFTERNOON YOU MEANT TO PHONE. Another: WHAT THE CAT SAW. Another, at ankle height, in letters so small she knelt: THE LAST THING YOU WILL FORGET ON PURPOSE. The doors were not locked. That seemed, somehow, like a test.

A librarian emerged through a revolving door that had not existed a moment before. He was young, or had decided to be young that morning, with ink on his cuffs and a pencil behind each ear. 'You're early,' he said. 'We aren't due to be discovered until Thursday.' Mara, who had survived forty years of council meetings, was not easily derailed. 'What is this place?' 'The Department of Unkept Things,' he said. 'Lost hours, abandoned plans, alternative Tuesdays. People misplace more life than they live, I'm afraid. We shelve what we can. The rest becomes weather.' He nodded at her tin. 'Ah. You've brought the town back.'

He explained, with the patience of a man accustomed to explaining tides to furniture, that every place occasionally slips its moorings and drifts toward what it might have been. Bridges appear. Dead mothers rehearse names in the wind. Rivers run back toward their sources, homesick. Usually the Department tidied it away by Thursday and no one remembered except in dreams. But the map had escaped. If Mara kept it unfolded until midnight, the town would stay as it was becoming: stranger, larger inside, haunted in useful ways. If she folded it now, everything would settle, safe and smaller.

Mara thought of her house, her grief, the vacant lot where a library might continue to exist. She thought of all the lives she had surveyed and measured and never quite entered, including her own. 'What do people usually choose?' she asked. 'Safety,' said the librarian. Outside, the wind said her name again, amused this time, and every door in the building leaned a fraction toward opening. Mara took the map from its tin and smoothed it flat.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A polished magical-realist fable about a town’s possible lives and one woman’s choice to keep them open.

## Grounded reading
The voice is whimsical and composed, with its strangeness delivered in practical, gently comic details: tea for “geography misbehaving,” maps that resent creases, and a river that declines to apologize. Beneath that lightness is real grief: Mara’s mother is “furniture” in her life, and the wind’s return of her voice makes loss newly immediate. The story invites the reader to treat memory and unrealized possibility not as errors to correct, but as forms of life worth making room for.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample centers on maps, rivers, doors, and other things that hold or redirect what might have been. It pairs mourning with curiosity, and sets the appeal of safety against a larger, stranger life. Mara’s final choice favors openness, even though the story does not promise that openness will be easy.

## Evidence line
> If Mara kept it unfolded until midnight, the town would stay as it was becoming: stranger, larger inside, haunted in useful ways.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring imagery and coherent movement from grief toward possibility give the story a distinctive imaginative signature, while its tightly shaped fable form concentrates that evidence in a single mode.
